messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The convoy had been moving through a narrow alley in Fallujah when the IED detonated. For Marcus, a 36-year-old tax consultant living in a quiet suburb of Denver, the memory is not a sequence of images but a sensory event. When it returns—and it returns often—he can taste the acrid, metallic dust that filled his mouth as the blast wave threw him against the armored vehicle’s interior. He remembers the silence that followed, a dense, unnatural quiet before the shouting began, and how that silence felt like a held breath before something worse. That specific quality of silence has never left him. Now, years later, when his wife goes quiet during an argument or when the office falls into a lull, Marcus feels his chest tighten. Unusual silence makes him feel something dangerous is about to happen, and he finds himself scanning the room for exits, noting the quickest path to the door before he can even think about what he is doing. He always identifies escape routes before he feels comfortable anywhere, a habit that has become as automatic as breathing.

The memory itself is overwhelming. When it surfaces, usually triggered by an unexpected confrontation or a conversation that veers too close to the war, Marcus feels so flooded with emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing. He will excuse himself from a meeting, go to the bathroom, and press his palms against the cool tile until the taste of dust fades. But the memory is inconsistent. Sometimes he can recall what happened but feels completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger. That detachment is almost worse, because it makes him feel broken, like a man watching his own life from a distance. He has come to believe that his emotions are dangerous, that feeling anything strongly—even happiness—is a trap. He pushes away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, a conviction that has made him distant from his wife and young daughter. He avoids talking with others about the event or its aftermath, and he has learned to steer conversations away from anything military, anything loud, anything that might pull the memory forward.

The triggers are specific and inescapable. Confrontations at work, even mild disagreements with a client about a tax deduction, feel like an ambush. Certain conversation topics—politics, news from the Middle East, even discussions about safety—send his mind reeling back to the alley. When he feels physically unwell, even a mild headache or an upset stomach, he immediately feels the threat of the memory closing in, as if his body is telling him that something is about to go wrong. In response, he has developed a strategy of avoidance that governs his daily life. He avoids any form of physical contact with others. When a colleague claps him on the shoulder, he reacts with alarm, his body jerking before his mind catches up. He has stopped shaking hands at networking events, a professional liability for a tax consultant who needs to build trust with clients. He has started working from home whenever possible, but even there, the silence of the house can feel threatening. He finds himself planning escape routes in restaurants, in the grocery store, in his own living room.

The cycle is tight and self-reinforcing. The triggers bring the memory, and the memory makes him feel threatened, which makes him hypervigilant to the next trigger. His avoidance strategies—pushing away feelings, avoiding touch, steering conversations—paradoxically make the triggers more potent because he never learns that they are safe. The taste of dust returns when he is stressed, and the stress of avoiding the memory makes the taste more vivid. He has begun to avoid his wife’s touch entirely, and she has started to ask him what is wrong. He cannot tell her. He does not have the words. What finally brought him to seek help was the moment his daughter, age four, reached for his hand and he flinched. He saw her face fall, and he knew that something in him was broken in a way that silence and escape routes could no longer hide. He is terrified that he will lose his family the way he lost his sense of safety, but he is equally afraid that talking about the memory will make it real again, that the taste of dust will never leave his mouth.
